summary: This unit teaches you to carry out a small piece of research for a salon or spa and to analyse what you find: set a clear aim and research question, plan methods, time and cost, choose primary and secondary sources and judge how reliable they are, design a questionnaire, choose a fair sample, collect and record data ethically, work out percentages and averages, choose a chart, and write a short, honest report with recommendations.

blocks.p: **Research** means finding out facts in an organised way so that you can make a decision. A salon owner who is thinking of opening on Sundays, adding a natural-hair service or changing her prices can guess, or she can find out. Research replaces guessing with facts.

This unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees. You will plan a small research project, collect information from clients and other sources, work out what it shows, and report it to the owner. The maths is simple: counting, percentages and averages. The harder part is being **honest, fair and careful**.

What this means in practice
rows: Write an aim, objectives and a clear research question
Choose methods, sources and a sample; set a deadline and budget
Tell primary from secondary and qualitative from quantitative data
Check whether a source is reliable; record where information came from
Design and test a questionnaire; interview, observe or tally
Choose a fair sample; get consent; protect privacy
Number forms; tally; enter in a spreadsheet; look for mistakes
Percentages, fractions, mean, median, mode, range and trends

flow: Decide what you need to find out

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks at the Centre. In the practicals your group plans and carries out a short client-needs survey (aim, questionnaire, tally, spreadsheet), then analyses a data pack of prices and sales and presents a one-page report. Do not collect names, phone numbers or addresses for practice work, and only survey people who agree.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: To decide whether to offer a new service, such as natural-hair care or men's grooming.
To set prices that clients will pay and that still earn a profit.
To choose opening hours that suit clients.
To understand clients' complaints, and to find out what competitors offer.
To make decisions from **facts**, not guesses or feelings.

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: The overall purpose of the research, in one sentence.
To find out whether clients in Mandeville would use and pay for a Saturday children's hair service.
A specific thing the research sets out to find. Each is measurable.
To find out how many clients have children aged 4 to 12; to find out what price parents would pay; to find which Saturday hours they prefer.
The question the research answers. It is clear, narrow and can be answered with facts.
Would clients with children use a Saturday children's service at about J$2,500?
A guess made before the research, which the research will test.
More than half of clients with children would use a Saturday children's service.

ul: The **first step** is to decide clearly what you need to find out. Without this, you collect a lot of information and none of it answers the owner's question.
A good question is not too wide ('What do clients want?') and not unanswerable ('Is our salon the best?'). It should be possible to answer with data.

blocks.p: Weak: 'Do people like salons?' Better: 'Would clients use a Sunday nail service?'

head: Part of the plan
What it says
rows: How you will collect the information: questionnaire, interview, observation, tally, secondary sources.
Which documents and which people: how many, from where, on which days.
Who does what and by when. The research must finish before the decision is made, for example before the new price list is printed.
Printing, travel, phone credit, time. Keep within a budget and keep receipts.
Who will receive it and in which form.

blocks.note: A **deadline** is the date by which the research must be finished. Work backwards from it. If the owner needs the findings in three weeks, you may have only one week for the survey.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Feature
Primary data
Secondary data
rows: New information that you collect yourself, for your own purpose.
Information that someone else has already collected.
A questionnaire to clients; an interview with a stylist; counting walk-ins for two weeks.
A government report on household spending; a trade magazine article; other salons' price lists; the salon's own sales records.
Up to date; about your own clients; answers your exact question.
Quicker and cheaper; may cover a large area or a long period.
Takes time and money to plan, collect and count.
May be out of date, may not answer your exact question, may be biased.

blocks.p: Good research usually uses both: secondary data first, to learn what is already known, then primary data to fill the gaps.

head: Type
Meaning
Example
rows: Data that can be counted or measured.
18 of 60 clients want Sunday opening; the average wait was 12 minutes.
Data in words: opinions, feelings and reasons.
'The staff are friendly, but it is hard to park.'

blocks.p: Quantitative data tells you **how many**; qualitative data tells you **why**. Use both.

head: Question
Why it matters
rows: Official bodies (for example the Statistical Institute of Jamaica, a government ministry, a university or a recognised trade association) are more reliable than an unnamed post.
An advert, a leaflet from a supplier or a paid post wants to sell. It may show only the good side.
Prices, trends and products change. Old information may no longer be true.
Is it based on facts that can be checked?
Figures, methods and sample sizes are stronger than phrases such as 'the best in Jamaica' or 'everyone says'.
Check at least two or three independent sources.

ul: Write down the author or organisation, the title, the date and where you found it (for example the web address).
You or others may need to check it again later, and you must give credit to the person who did the work.
At the end of the report, list all sources: this is the **bibliography**.

blocks.note: When you collect prices from other salons, note the date and the exact service. A 'wash and set' at one salon may include a treatment; at another it may not.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Collecting information: questionnaires and other methods

head: Method
How it works
Good for
Weakness
rows: A set of written questions answered by many people.
People may skip or misread questions; little detail.
You ask questions face to face or by phone.
Takes time; fewer people; the interviewer's manner may influence answers.
Watching and recording what people do, for example how many walk-ins arrive each day.
Finding out what people actually do, not what they say.
Takes time; the observer may notice only some things.
Marking each count as it happens, in groups of five.
Needs someone to keep counting accurately.
A small group is brought together to discuss a topic.
Opinions and ideas; hearing people react to each other.
Reading existing reports, price lists and records.

blocks.p: To count with a **tally chart**, make one mark for each answer, and cross every fifth mark through the four: ||||. Count in fives afterwards.

ul: Begin with the **aim**. Every question must help to answer it. If it does not, leave it out.
Keep it **short**: about 8 to 10 questions, so that people finish it.
At the top, say what it is for, how long it takes, that taking part is **their choice** and that answers are private.
Use simple, clear words, and ask **one thing at a time**. 'Are you happy with our prices and our opening hours?' asks two things.
Most questions should be **closed** (tick boxes, yes/no, rating scale 1 to 5), because they are quick to answer and easy to count. Add one or two **open** questions for comments.
Put easy questions first.
**Test it** on a few people first (a pilot). Fix anything they do not understand.

head: Question type
Example
Used for
rows: 'Would you use a Sunday nail service?'  Yes / No / Not sure
'Which time suits you best?'  Morning / Afternoon / Evening
Easy to count; shows strength of opinion
'What one service would you like us to add?'

head: Problem
Bad question
Better question
rows: 'Don't you agree our prices are the best?'
'How would you rate our prices: too high, about right, or low?'
'How many times a month do you visit?'  1 / 2 to 3 / 4 or more
'Do you want a deep-conditioning protein treatment?'
'Do you want a treatment to strengthen your hair?'

blocks.note: A leading question makes the result worthless, because the owner learns only what she already believed. Always check each question: does it push the person towards an answer?
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Choosing a sample and following research ethics

blocks.p: A **sample** is the group of people chosen to take part. You cannot ask everybody, so you ask a smaller group that stands for all of them. If the sample does not stand for the whole group, the results can be wrong. This is called **bias**.

head: Problem
Why the results are wrong
What to do instead
rows: Asking only friends or the best clients
They may say what you want to hear.
Ask a mix of clients, chosen without favour.
You miss workers who come in the evenings and older clients who come midweek.
Survey on different days and at different times.
One or two opinions may be unusual.
Ask enough people: at least 30 to 50 for a small salon.
Asking only people who answer quickly
Those who need help or are shy are left out.

ul: Decide the sample in the plan, before you collect any data.
The group you ask should match the group the research is about. If it is about clients who have children, ask clients who have children.
A bigger, mixed sample is more trustworthy than a small, similar one.

blocks.p: **Ethics** means doing research honestly and fairly, and respecting people.

ul: **Consent:** tell people what the research is for, how the answers will be used and how long it will take. Make clear taking part is a free choice. Never pressure anyone, for example by hinting that she may lose her booking.

**Privacy:** ask only for personal details that you really need. Do not ask for names if you do not need them. Keep forms and computer files locked away or protected by a password. Under Jamaica's Data Protection Act, people's personal information must be kept safe and used only for its purpose.
**Honesty:** report what you find, even if the owner will not like it. Never leave out results or change figures. Give credit to the sources you used.
**Fair treatment:** do not give gifts or hints that push people towards a particular answer.
**Respect:** thank people for their time. Do not ask offensive or too personal questions.

blocks.note: If the results show something unwelcome, such as clients unhappy with cleanliness, the report must still say so. A research report that hides bad news is useless to the owner and dishonest.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: When you survey at the Centre for practice work, ask only people who agree, and do not collect names, phone numbers or addresses.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Check every form for missing or unclear answers
Set up a table or spreadsheet

ul: **Number the forms** (1, 2, 3 ...) so you can find any form again and none is counted twice.
**Check each form.** Decide how to treat a missing answer, for example as 'no answer'. Do not guess what someone meant.
In a **spreadsheet**, make one row for each form and one column for each question. Enter the ticked answer or the rating score.
For open questions, type the comments and then group similar ones under headings such as 'prices', 'waiting time' and 'parking'.
A spreadsheet adds up and sorts large amounts of data quickly and can draw charts. A tally chart on paper is good for small counts.

**Check for mistakes** before you analyse: look for entries that are impossible (a rating of 7 on a scale of 1 to 5), numbers typed wrongly, and rows entered twice. Ask a partner to check a sample of your entries.
Add up each column and compare with the number of forms. If 40 forms were collected, the answers to each closed question must add up to 40 (plus any 'no answer').

head: Form no.
Q1: Would you use Sunday opening?
Q2: Rating of service (1 to 5)

blocks.note: Keep completed forms in a locked folder or cabinet, away from the reception desk, so that no one else can read them.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: To turn a count into a **percentage**, divide the number by the total and multiply by 100.

ul: 45 of 150 clients want Sunday opening: 45 ÷ 150 = 0.30, and 0.30 × 100 = **30%**.
Check: all the percentages for one question must add up to 100%.
Fractions: 3 out of 12 is 3/12, which in its simplest form is **1/4** (divide top and bottom by 3). 1/4 is 25%.

blocks.p: Imagine five clients waited 8, 12, 12, 20 and 18 minutes.

head: Measure
How to find it
Result
rows: Add all the values and divide by how many there are: (8 + 12 + 12 + 20 + 18) ÷ 5 = 70 ÷ 5
Put in order: 8, 12, 12, 18, 20. The middle one is the third.
The value that appears most often.

ul: If there is an **even** number of values, the median is halfway between the two middle ones: for 4, 6, 8, 10 the median is (6 + 8) ÷ 2 = 7.
The mean can be pulled up by one very high value. The median is then a better 'typical' value.
A **large range** means the values are very different from each other.
**Share:** hair services made J$120,000 of J$300,000 total sales. 120,000 ÷ 300,000 = 0.4 = 40% of sales.
**Change:** sales went from J$80,000 to J$100,000. The increase is J$20,000. 20,000 ÷ 80,000 = 0.25 = **25% increase**.
**Trend:** the general pattern over time. Monthly sales of J$80,000, J$95,000 and J$110,000 show a rising trend.
A **finding** says what the data shows, in plain words: 'Over half of the clients (55%) want Sunday opening.'
Say how many people answered. Always give the total (40 clients).
Report all the results, including those the owner may not like.
Do not say more than the data shows. 'Most clients want Sunday opening' is true only if more than half do.
A **recommendation** is a suggested action based on the findings, for example 'Try opening on two Sundays a month and review the takings.'

blocks.note: Work every calculation twice, or ask a partner to check it. One slip in a percentage or an average can lead to a wrong recommendation.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Chart
What it shows
Use it for
Example
rows: Prices of a wash and set at five salons; the number of clients for hair, nails and skin
Showing the share of a whole (the parts add up to 100%). Not too many slices.
What share of sales came from hair, nails, skin and retail

ul: Every chart needs a **title**, labels on the axes (the x-axis is the line along the bottom, and the y-axis is the line up the side) and units (J$, minutes, number of clients).
Keep the chart simple, with clear colours and no extra decoration.
In a pie chart, 25% is a quarter of the circle (90 degrees).
Say in a sentence what the chart shows.

blocks.h: A short research report for the owner

flow: Summary of main findings and recommendations

head: Part
What goes in it
rows: So the report can be found and understood later.
Two or three sentences, so that a busy owner can read the main points first.
What the research set out to find out.
How the information was collected: for example a questionnaire to 50 clients over two weeks, and the price lists of five salons.
The results in plain words, with simple tables or charts and percentages or averages. Honest, including unwelcome results.
Practical actions that follow from the findings, with reasons. Two or three are enough.

ul: Use short sentences and plain words.
Separate **facts** (what the data shows) from **opinions** (what people think or what you think).
Present the report politely to the owner and be ready to answer questions about how you got the results.

blocks.note: Many Jamaican salon owners are very busy. A one-page report with a clear summary at the top is more likely to be read and used than a long one.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can explain why a salon does research and why it matters to use facts.
I can write an aim, objectives and a clear research question.
I can write a research plan with methods, sample, deadline and cost.
I can tell primary from secondary data, and quantitative from qualitative data.
I can judge whether a source is reliable and record where information came from.
I can design a questionnaire with clear, closed and open questions and no leading questions.
I can test a questionnaire before using it.
I can explain what a sample is, and how to avoid bias.
I can follow research ethics: consent, privacy and honesty.
I can record, check and organise data in a tally chart or spreadsheet.
I can work out percentages, fractions, mean, median, mode and range.
I can describe a trend and a share.
I can choose a bar chart, a pie chart or a line graph for the data.
I can write a short, honest report with findings and recommendations.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give a reason for each step. For example: 'I test the questionnaire on a few people first, so that I can find questions that people do not understand.'
blocks.label: Tip

Information collected but not yet sorted or analysed.
A set of written questions for people to answer.
A person who answers a survey.
A question that people answer freely in their own words.
A question that pushes people towards a certain answer.
The group of people chosen to take part.
A sample or a result that is unfair or one-sided.
A small group brought together to discuss a topic.
A nearby business offering the same services.
A way to count using marks in fives.

c1.title: A children's service in Mandeville
c1.text: Mrs. Hyacinth Morgan owns a salon in Mandeville. She is thinking of offering a Saturday service for children aged 4 to 12, and wants to know if parents would use it and what they would pay. She needs the answer in three weeks, before she orders supplies. She has J$4,000 for printing and phone credit. A trainee, Rushane, offers to help.

c2.title: A survey of new services
c2.text: A salon in Savanna-la-Mar asked 80 clients one question: 'Which new service would you most like us to add?' The answers were: natural-hair care 28; men's grooming 20; children's cuts 16; nothing new 16.

c3.title: What do the other salons charge?
c3.text: A trainee, Shanelle, phones five salons in Montego Bay and records their prices for a wash and set on the same day: J$2,800, J$3,500, J$3,000, J$4,200 and J$3,500. The salon she is working for charges J$3,800.

c4.title: Which source can we trust?
c4.text: A trainee is researching what clients spend on hair care. She finds (a) a supplier's leaflet that says '9 out of 10 stylists prefer our products'; (b) an unsigned blog post from 2016 listing salon prices; (c) this year's report by a recognised trade association, with named authors and a note on how the survey was done.

c5.title: Surveying clients in the waiting area
c5.text: Trainee Kemoy hands out questionnaires to clients in a salon's waiting area. One client asks, 'Who will see my answers?' Another form is left lying on the reception desk. The supervisor suggests giving a free sample to clients who tick 'excellent' for service.

questions.q: Which is the clearest research question for Mrs. Morgan?
o: Do the people of Mandeville enjoy going to hair salons in general?
Is Mrs. Morgan's salon better than the other salons in town?
Would parents use a Saturday children's service at about J$2,500?
What do children think about their hair and their hairstyles?
questions.why: A good question is narrow and can be answered with facts: who, what service, which price. The others are too wide or cannot be answered with data.

questions.q: Which sample would give Mrs. Morgan the fairest answer?
o: Parents of clients, asked on different days and times
Only the parents who come to the salon on Saturday morning
Parents who ask for the most expensive services at the salon
Her own relatives who have young children at home
questions.why: A fair sample matches the group the research is about and is mixed. Relatives may say what she wants to hear, and one day or one kind of client leaves others out.

questions.q: What should Rushane do before he prints 60 questionnaires?
o: Add more questions so that the questionnaire looks more serious
Print them all at once, to save money on a second printing
Ask the owner's close friends to fill them in and say what they think
Test it on two or three parents and correct confusing questions
questions.why: A pilot shows questions that people misunderstand before it is too late. Printing straight away risks wasting the J$4,000, and a long form is less likely to be finished.

questions.q: What percentage of the 80 clients chose natural-hair care?
questions.why: 28 ÷ 80 = 0.35, so 35%. As a check, the four answers are 35%, 25%, 20% and 20%, which add up to 100%.

questions.q: Which statement is supported by the results?
o: Nearly everyone is happy with the present services
The largest group, 35%, want natural-hair care
Men's grooming is the most popular new service
Most clients want natural-hair care
questions.why: 35% is the largest group but not more than half, so 'most' is wrong. 80% chose a new service, so it cannot be said that nearly everyone is happy, and natural-hair care, not men's grooming, leads.

questions.q: Which chart is best for showing each answer as a share of all the answers?
o: A spreadsheet
A line graph
A tally chart
A pie chart
questions.why: A pie chart shows how a whole is divided into shares. A line graph shows change over time, and a tally chart and a spreadsheet are tools for counting and recording, not for showing shares.

questions.q: Which recommendation follows best from the findings?
o: Try natural-hair care as a trial and review the bookings
Start natural-hair care in full next week, as most clients want it
Add nothing, since 16 clients want nothing new
Start children's cuts first, because it is the cheapest to begin
questions.why: 35% is the largest group, but not a majority, so a trial and a review is a sensible, evidence-based step. Starting in full rests on a wrong 'most', and adding nothing ignores the 80% who want something new.

questions.q: What is the mean price of a wash and set at the five salons?
What are the median and the mode of the five prices?
o: Median J$3,500 and mode J$4,200
Median J$3,400 and mode J$3,500
Median J$3,000 and mode J$3,500
Median J$3,500 and mode J$3,500
questions.why: In order the prices are 2,800, 3,000, 3,500, 3,500 and 4,200. The middle (third) value is 3,500, and 3,500 appears twice, so it is also the mode.

questions.q: What do the figures suggest about Shanelle's salon, which charges J$3,800?
o: It charges above the mean and median, so the owner should look at why
It charges the lowest price in town, so it can safely raise its price now
Its price is exactly the same as the typical price charged in the town
The figures are useless, because only five salons were asked about prices
questions.why: J$3,800 is above the mean (J$3,400) and the median (J$3,500). That is a fact to report; the owner then considers why clients still come. A small sample limits how far results can be trusted, but does not make them useless.

questions.q: What is the range of the five prices?
questions.why: Range is the highest minus the lowest: 4,200 − 2,800 = 1,400.

questions.q: Which source is the most reliable for the report?
o: All three are equally reliable, as long as they agree with her idea
The trade association's report from this year
The supplier's leaflet, because it has the most numbers in it
The unsigned blog post from 2016, because it lists salon prices
questions.why: Named authors, a clear method and a recent date make it checkable. The leaflet wants to sell, and the blog is unsigned and out of date.

questions.q: Why should she be cautious about the claim '9 out of 10 stylists prefer our products'?
o: It is from the seller and does not say who was asked or how many
Leaflets from suppliers are never printed with correct figures in them
Stylists are not able to compare one product with another
Percentages from a survey cannot be used in a research report
questions.why: A seller wants to sell, and the claim gives no sample size or method, so it cannot be checked. Always ask who was asked, how many and by whom.

questions.q: What should the trainee write down about each source she uses?
o: Only the web address, since that is enough to find it again
Nothing, since she can look the sources up again if she needs them
Author, title, date and where she found it
Only the title, to keep her notes short and tidy
questions.why: Author, title, date and place let anyone check the information and give credit. The details also form the bibliography.

questions.q: What should Kemoy tell the client who asks who will see her answers?
o: The owner and the other clients, to show what they think
Only the survey team, and no names will be on the report
The whole salon, since everybody wants to know what clients think
Nobody at all, ever, so she has no need to worry
questions.why: People have a right to know how their answers will be used. Be honest about who sees them, and do not promise more than you can do.

questions.q: What is wrong with the completed form left on the reception desk?
o: Nothing, since the form has no names on it
It will get dirty and the writing may fade in the light
It should be handed to the owner to read straight away
Anyone could read it, so it belongs in a locked folder
questions.why: Completed forms are private. Keep them safe, because even forms without names may contain personal information.

questions.q: Why is the supervisor's idea of a free sample for clients who tick 'excellent' a problem?
o: Clients may not like the sample products that are being given
Free products are not allowed to be handed out in any salon
It pushes clients towards one answer, so results are biased
It costs too much for a salon of this size to give them out
questions.why: Rewarding a particular answer is not honest research. The owner would get a false picture.

questions.q: Which question asks two different things at once, and so should be split?
o: Which day of the week do you find easiest to visit us?
Is the salon clean and friendly?
How would you rate the cleanliness of our salon?
How many times a month do you visit the salon?
questions.why: A question should ask one thing at a time. 'Clean and friendly' are two ideas, and a client may feel differently about each, so the answers cannot be counted properly.

questions.q: Six clients waited 4, 6, 6, 8, 10 and 16 minutes. What is the median?
o: 8 minutes
6 minutes
8.3 minutes
7 minutes
questions.why: In order the values are 4, 6, 6, 8, 10 and 16. There are six, so the median is halfway between the third and fourth: (6 + 8) ÷ 2 = 7.

questions.q: Monthly sales were J$80,000, then J$100,000. What was the percentage increase?
questions.why: The increase is J$20,000. 20,000 ÷ 80,000 = 0.25, which is 25% of the starting figure.
